Science fiction does not always need to be traveling through space or going into battle in another galaxy. Sometimes, the most fascinating sci-fi stories are the ones with a single extraordinary idea set in our world. Many classify these movies as soft science fiction. By putting less emphasis on the spectacle and speculative concepts, these movies can tell surprisingly intimate stories, while also working in the sci-fi framework.

Here, we take a look at some of the soft sci-fi movies that are practically perfect. The films on this list execute their concepts with flying colors, with some even becoming classics in the genre as well. Most interestingly, these movies prove that you don't need a gigantic budget for production design or CGI just to tell a compelling sci-fi story. With their premise, they know exactly what kind of story they want to tell, and they succeed.

'The Vast of Night' (2019)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/the-vast-of-night2.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
blocks.c: A scene from The Vast of Night.

blocks.x: Image via Amazon Studios

The Vast of Night takes place in a small New Mexico town, where a teenage radio DJ named Everett (Jake Horowitz) and a young switchboard operator named Fay (Sierra McCormick) are working during an ordinary evening. Their night changes when they notice a strange sound appearing on the network. The two begin investigating the mysterious transmission and eventually hear callers describing unexplained experiences involving strange lights and unidentified objects.

The Vast of Night's greatest trick is turning limitations into strengths. It builds its mystery through sound and suggestion, letting the audience's imagination fill in the rest. The long takes and extended conversations also provide tension on their own, showing the events happening in real time. Most importantly, The Vast of Night understands that uncertainty can be more frightening than explanation. It follows the old adage of "show, don't tell," and it does it effectively. Nevertheless, it's still an underseen film that's waiting to be seen by more people.
'The Assessment' (2024)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/the-assessment-elizabeth-olsen-himesh-patel.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
blocks.c: Elizbeth Olsen as Mia sitting on the couch next to Himesh Patel as Aaryan in The Assessment

blocks.x: Image via Magnolia Pictures

The Assessment follows Mia (Elizabeth Olsen) and Aaryan (Himesh Patel), a successful couple who decide that they want to become parents. Having children is a privilege in this future, so they must be evaluated by a government assessor named Virginia (Alicia Vikander). The structured examination gradually becomes invasive as Virginia inserts herself into their home and assumes different roles to test their responses, relationship, and ability to parent.

The Assessment might be the newest film on this list, but it does not diminish the fact that it is a stellar soft sci-fi effort. The premise feels simultaneously futuristic and uncomfortably familiar. Olsen, Patel, and Vikander give their characters very different forms of emotional tension, particularly as Virginia becomes genuinely unpredictable. Most importantly, the movie leaves room for ambiguity about where institutional control ends and personal responsibility begins. The Assessment is also notable for being the debut script for its screenwriters and the debut feature film for director Fleur Fortuné.
'Chronicle' (2012)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/chronicle-michael-b-jordan-dane-de-haan.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
blocks.c: Michael B. Jordan, Dane De Haan, and Alex Russell sit around a library table in Chronicle

blocks.x: Image via 20th Century Studios

Chronicle follows Andrew Detmer (Dane DeHaan), a troubled teenager who begins documenting his life with a camera while struggling with family problems. Alongside his cousin Matt (Alex Russell) and classmate Steve (Michael B. Jordan), Andrew discovers a mysterious underground object that gives them abilities. At first, their powers are simply exciting, but Andrew's emotional problems make his powers dangerous.

Chronicle is the soft sci-fi take on the superhero origin story in the form of a grounded character study. The found footage format, which was all the rage in the 2010s, brings the audience closer to the trio, especially Andrew. The film builds up Andrew's backstory really well, so it never feels out of place when he turns into a bad person. DeHaan gives a breakthrough performance, while Michael B. Jordan steals every scene. In a landscape filled with superhero movies from Marvel and DC, it's easy to forget Chronicle, yet it is still one of the most effective offerings in the genre.
'Never Let Me Go' (2010)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/neverletmego.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
blocks.c: Ruth, Tommy and Kathy, played by Keira Knightley, Andrew Garfield and Carey Mulligan, stand by a river looking somber in Never Let Me Go.

blocks.x: Image via 20th Century Studios

Never Let Me Go follows Kathy (Carey Mulligan), Tommy (Andrew Garfield), and Ruth (Keira Knightley), three friends who grow up together at a secluded boarding school named Hailsham. Raised from a young age there, they eventually learn that they were created as clones whose purpose is to donate their organs to others. As they grow older and have relationships, the reality of their predetermined futures becomes impossible to ignore.

Based on an acclaimed sci-fi novel by Kazuo Ishiguro, Never Let Me Go is a quietly devastating soft sci-fi film, the quiet and meditative sibling of The Island. Unlike the bombastic journey the characters go through in Michael Bay's film, here, the clones rarely revolt because the system has conditioned them from childhood to accept their fate, which makes the story's horror feel disturbing. The main characters, however, still worry about love, jealousy, friendship, and whether they have lived meaningful lives, even though society has already decided what their lives are worth.
'Midnight Special' (2016)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2023/02/jaeden-martell-and-michael-shannon-in-midnight-special.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
blocks.c: Roy kneeling down to talk to Alton in Midnight Special

blocks.x: Image via Warner Bros. Pictures

Midnight Special centers on Alton (Jaeden Martell), a young boy who possesses extraordinary abilities. His father Roy (Michael Shannon) desperately tries to protect him while keeping him hidden from both the government and a religious group that believes the boy has a special connection to their faith. The film also stars Kirsten Dunst, Joel Edgerton, and Adam Driver.

Directed by Jeff Nichols, who has helmed a number of acclaimed indie films like Take Shelter and Mud, Midnight Special is practically flawless in the way it balances its mystery with the film's central emotions, gradually revealing Alton's powers to keep audiences engaged. The government investigation, religious interpretation, and science-fiction explanation all provide different attempts to understand what Alton's powers mean. Leading a great ensemble, Shannon gives a stellar performance in this forgotten sci-fi film that deserves to be rediscovered today.

Which Sci-Fi Hero Are You Most Like?
Paul Atreides · Captain Kirk · Princess Leia · Ellen Ripley · Max Rockatansky

Five iconic heroes. Five completely different ways of facing an impossible universe. One of them shares your instincts, your values, and your particular way of refusing to back down. Eight questions will tell you which one.

🖖Capt. Kirk
✊Princess Leia
🔦Ellen Ripley
🔥Max Rockatansky
FIND YOUR HERO →

How do you lead when the stakes couldn't be higher?
The way you lead under pressure is the most honest thing about you.

AI absorb everything — every variable, every pattern — and move only when I know the path forward.
BI read the room, make the call, and own the consequences. Hesitation costs more than mistakes.
CI rally people. A cause needs a voice, and I refuse to let fear be louder than conviction.
DI assess the threat, establish what needs doing, and get it done without waiting for permission.
EI don't lead. I act. Others can follow or not — I'm already moving.
NEXT QUESTION →

What is your greatest strength in a crisis?
The quality that keeps you alive when everything else fails.

APrescience — the ability to see further ahead than anyone else and plan accordingly.
BImprovisation — I'm at my best when the plan falls apart and I have to invent a new one.
CConviction — I know what I'm fighting for, and that certainty doesn't waver under fire.
DComposure — I stay functional when everyone around me is falling apart. Panic is a luxury.
EEndurance — I outlast things. I take the hit and keep moving long after others have stopped.
NEXT QUESTION →

What is the thing you'd sacrifice everything else for?
Your deepest motivation is your truest compass.

AThe survival and dignity of my people — even if I have to become something frightening to ensure it.
BThe safety of my crew — every single one of them. No one gets left behind.
CFreedom — for my people, for every world still crushed under the weight of an empire.
DThe truth — what actually happened, what's actually out there, whether anyone believes me or not.
EThe one person — or the one memory — that still makes any of this worth surviving for.
NEXT QUESTION →

How do you relate to the people around you?
Who you are to others under pressure is who you really are.

AWith intensity and distance — I care deeply, but the weight I carry makes closeness complicated.
BWith warmth and irreverence — I take the mission seriously, not myself.
CWith directness and trust — I say what I mean, and I expect the people I work with to rise to it.
DWith professional care but clear limits — I'll protect you, but I won't pretend we're family.
EWith wariness that slowly becomes loyalty — I don't trust easily, but when I do, it holds.
NEXT QUESTION →

You're facing a threat that no one else believes is real. What do you do?
How you respond when you're the only one who sees it defines everything.

APrepare in silence. If they won't listen, I'll be ready when they finally have to.
BKeep pushing until someone listens — and if no one does, handle it myself.
CBuild the case, find the allies, and make the threat impossible to ignore.
DDocument everything. The truth matters even if no one believes it yet.
EStop trying to convince anyone. Survive it. That's the only argument that counts.
NEXT QUESTION →

What has your heroism cost you personally?
Every hero pays. The question is what — and whether they'd pay it again.

AMy innocence — I've seen what I'm capable of, and I can't unsee it.
BPeople I loved — the command chair has a view, but it's a lonely one.
CA normal life — I gave up everything ordinary the moment I chose the cause.
DMy sense of safety — I know exactly what's out there now, and I can't pretend otherwise.
EAlmost everything — and I'm still not sure what I'm carrying it all for. But I keep going.
NEXT QUESTION →

How do you feel about the rules of the world you're in?
Every hero has a relationship with the system. What's yours?

AI understand them deeply — and I know exactly which ones must be broken, and why.
BI respect the spirit of them and bend the letter when the situation demands it.
CThe system is the problem. I'm not here to work within it — I'm here to dismantle it.
DI follow protocol until protocol stops being useful. Then I make the call myself.
EThe rules collapsed a long time ago. What's left is instinct, and mine are reliable.
NEXT QUESTION →

When everything is on the line, what keeps you going?
The answer is the most honest thing about you.

ADestiny — or something that feels so much like it that the difference no longer matters.
BThe people on my ship — their faces, their trust, the fact that they're counting on me.
CThe belief that what we're fighting for is worth every sacrifice, including this one.
DSheer refusal to let it win — whatever it is. I don't stop. That's just who I am.
EI'm not sure anymore. But the road is still there, and I'm still on it.
REVEAL MY HERO →

Your Hero Has Been Identified
Your Sci-Fi Hero Is…
Your answers point to the iconic sci-fi hero who shares your instincts, your values, and your particular way of facing the impossible.
Arrakis · Dune
Paul Atreides
You carry a weight most people would crumble under — the knowledge of what you're capable of, and the burden of what you might have to become.
You see further ahead than others and you plan accordingly, even when the vision frightens you.
You are driven by loyalty to your people and a sense of destiny you didn't ask for but can't escape.
Paul Atreides is not simply a hero — he is someone who understands the cost of power and chooses to bear it anyway.
That gravity, that willingness to carry what others won't, is exactly you.
USS Enterprise · Star Trek
Captain Kirk
You lead with instinct, warmth, and an absolute refusal to accept a no-win scenario — because you've always believed there's a third option nobody else has thought of yet.
You take the mission seriously without ever taking yourself too seriously.
Your crew would follow you anywhere, not because you demand it, but because you've earned it.
Kirk's genius isn't tactical — it's human. He reads people, bends rules with purpose, and wills outcomes into existence through sheer conviction.
That combination of warmth, audacity, and relentless optimism is unmistakably yours.
The Rebellion · Star Wars
Princess Leia
You are the kind of person who holds the line when everyone else is losing faith — not because you're fearless, but because giving up simply isn't something you're capable of.
You lead through conviction. Your voice carries because your belief is unshakeable.
You gave up everything ordinary the moment you chose the cause, and you've never looked back.
Leia is not a supporting character in her own story — she is the moral centre of the entire rebellion.
That same fierce, principled, unbreakable core is what defines you.
The Nostromo · Alien
Ellen Ripley
You are not reckless, not grandiose, and not particularly interested in being anyone's hero — you just refuse to stop when it matters.
You see threats clearly, you document the truth even when no one listens, and when the time comes you handle it yourself.
Ripley's heroism is earned, not performed. She doesn't have a speech — she has a flamethrower and a plan.
You share her composure under the worst possible pressure, and her refusal to pretend the monster isn't there.
When it counts, you don't flinch. That's everything.
The Wasteland · Mad Max
Max Rockatansky
You have been through fire that would break most people — and what came out the other side is something the world underestimates at its peril.
You don't ask for help, don't need validation, and don't wait for anyone to tell you the rules no longer apply.
Your loyalty, when it finally arrives, is absolute — but it's earned in silence and tested in action, not in words.
Max is not a nihilist. He is someone who lost everything and found, against his will, that he still has something worth protecting.
That bruised, stubborn, ultimately human core is exactly yours.

'10 Cloverfield Lane' (2016)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/mary-elizabeth-winstead-and-john-godoman-in-10-cloverfield-lane.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
blocks.c: A scared Michelle pressing her body against a door to stop Dan from entering in 10 Cloverfield Lane

blocks.x: Image via Paramount Pictures

10 Cloverfield Lane follows Michelle (Mary Elizabeth Winstead), who wakes up after an accident inside an underground bunker belonging to a mysterious man named Howard (John Goodman). He tells her that the outside world has become uninhabitable following a catastrophic attack and insists that staying inside the bunker is the only way she can survive. But Michelle suspects that Howard is not telling the whole truth.

10 Cloverfield Lane leans more into psychological thriller than the other films on this list. For most of its runtime, it barely needs conventional sci-fi elements because the uncertainty surrounding the outside world is already enough to generate tension. John Goodman's terrifying, increasingly unhinged performance as Howard is crucial, while Mary Elizabeth Winstead's Michelle joins a long line of great protagonists in the sci-fi-thriller genre. When the third act hits, it fulfills every sci-fi fan's dreams. It might have the Cloverfield connection, but it works great as a standalone film.
'Coherence' (2013)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/coherence-emily-baldoni-1.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
blocks.c: A man and a woman in Coherence

blocks.x: Image via Oscilloscope Laboratories

Coherence follows a group of friends who gather for a dinner party on the same night a comet passes unusually close to Earth. The ordinary evening quickly becomes unsettling when the power goes out, and they discover that something strange is happening outside. A nearby house appears to be identical to theirs, and as the group investigates, they begin encountering alternate versions of themselves.

Coherence may be the film with the lowest budget on this list, but it can still hold its own against the genre's heavyweights. The confined house becomes a perfect setting for the increasingly complicated reality, while the fragmented conversations and improvised performances add a surreal quality that puts the audience in the characters' headspace. Every element in the film, from the setting, editing, and mood, contributes to the uneasy atmosphere. The whole film feels like a puzzle, and it gets better with every rewatch.
'Under the Skin' (2013)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2022/08/Under-The-Skin---Scarlett-Johansson.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
blocks.c: The Alien, played by Scarlett Johansson, drives by a man in the film Under the Skin.

blocks.x: Image via A24

Under the Skin follows an extraterrestrial played by Scarlett Johansson who takes the form of a woman and travels through Scotland, approaching men she encounters along the way. She seduces them into following her to an isolated location, where they are subjected to a bizarre and horrifying fate. As she continues interacting with humans and becomes exposed to ordinary experiences, something changes in her.

Jonathan Glazer's Under the Skin keeps its mystery by not explaining its alien protagonist because it would undermine the fundamental feeling of alienation that defines the movie. Johansson gives one of her best performances with a restrained approach to the character. The hypnotic visuals, unsettling sound design, minimalist dialogue, and haunting score create an otherworldly experience that feels fundamentally different from other sci-fi films. It is soft sci-fi at its most uncompromising, using an extraterrestrial premise to explore humanity by looking at it from the outside.
'Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind' (2004)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/eternal-sunshine.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
blocks.c: Jim Carrey as Joel and Kate Winslet as Clementine laying in the snow in Eternal Sunshine of a Spotless Mind.

blocks.x: Image via Focus Features

Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind follows Joel (Jim Carrey), who discovers that his former girlfriend, Clementine (Kate Winslet), has undergone a procedure to erase every memory of their relationship. Hurt and confused, Joel decides to have the same procedure performed on himself. However, as his memories begin disappearing, he realizes that he does not actually want to forget Clementine.

Charlie Kaufman is no stranger to surreal and trippy stories. Paired with Michel Gondry's imaginative vision, Eternal Sunshine is the perfect marriage between romance and science fiction. The memory erasure plot is used as a representation of something people already do emotionally, like trying to escape painful experiences rather than accepting them. Even the structure mirrors the film's argument that by watching memories disappear, the audience comes to understand their value at the same time Joel does. Carrey turns in one of the best performances of his career, in a rare dramatic turn, and Winslet's Clementine is complex and interesting. It's not only one of the best sci-fi of the 21st century, but one of the best films ever.
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/her-2013.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
blocks.c: Joaquin Phoenix looking sad and contemplative in front of a computer screen in Her (2013)

blocks.x: Image via Warner Bros. Pictures

Her follows Theodore Twombly (Joaquin Phoenix), a lonely writer struggling to move on from the breakdown of his marriage. His life changes when he gets an advanced operating system with an artificial intelligence named Samantha (Scarlett Johansson), an intelligent AI who develops a distinct personality and forms a romantic relationship with him.

Despite being released more than a decade ago, Her feels more relevant today. With AI now becoming ubiquitous in our lives, this film eerily predicts our current situation. The world is familiar and not too futuristic, a believable extension of contemporary society rather than an artificial science-fiction setting. Phoenix and Johansson also create a convincing relationship despite the fact that one character is never physically present in the traditional sense. Visually, Her is beautiful to watch, and it won Spike Jonze Best Original Screenplay at the Oscars.

'10 Cloverfield Lane' (2016)

Image via Paramount Pictures

10 Cloverfield Lane follows Michelle (Mary Elizabeth Winstead), who wakes up after an accident inside an underground bunker belonging to a mysterious man named Howard (John Goodman). He tells her that the outside world has become uninhabitable following a catastrophic attack and insists that staying inside the bunker is the only way she can survive. But Michelle suspects that Howard is not telling the whole truth.

10 Cloverfield Lane leans more into psychological thriller than the other films on this list. For most of its runtime, it barely needs conventional sci-fi elements because the uncertainty surrounding the outside world is already enough to generate tension. John Goodman's terrifying, increasingly unhinged performance as Howard is crucial, while Mary Elizabeth Winstead's Michelle joins a long line of great protagonists in the sci-fi-thriller genre. When the third act hits, it fulfills every sci-fi fan's dreams. It might have the Cloverfield connection, but it works great as a standalone film.

'Coherence' (2013)

Image via Oscilloscope Laboratories

Coherence follows a group of friends who gather for a dinner party on the same night a comet passes unusually close to Earth. The ordinary evening quickly becomes unsettling when the power goes out, and they discover that something strange is happening outside. A nearby house appears to be identical to theirs, and as the group investigates, they begin encountering alternate versions of themselves.

Coherence may be the film with the lowest budget on this list, but it can still hold its own against the genre's heavyweights. The confined house becomes a perfect setting for the increasingly complicated reality, while the fragmented conversations and improvised performances add a surreal quality that puts the audience in the characters' headspace. Every element in the film, from the setting, editing, and mood, contributes to the uneasy atmosphere. The whole film feels like a puzzle, and it gets better with every rewatch.

'Under the Skin' (2013)

Image via A24

Under the Skin follows an extraterrestrial played by Scarlett Johansson who takes the form of a woman and travels through Scotland, approaching men she encounters along the way. She seduces them into following her to an isolated location, where they are subjected to a bizarre and horrifying fate. As she continues interacting with humans and becomes exposed to ordinary experiences, something changes in her.

Jonathan Glazer's Under the Skin keeps its mystery by not explaining its alien protagonist because it would undermine the fundamental feeling of alienation that defines the movie. Johansson gives one of her best performances with a restrained approach to the character. The hypnotic visuals, unsettling sound design, minimalist dialogue, and haunting score create an otherworldly experience that feels fundamentally different from other sci-fi films. It is soft sci-fi at its most uncompromising, using an extraterrestrial premise to explore humanity by looking at it from the outside.

'Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind' (2004)

Image via Focus Features

Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind follows Joel (Jim Carrey), who discovers that his former girlfriend, Clementine (Kate Winslet), has undergone a procedure to erase every memory of their relationship. Hurt and confused, Joel decides to have the same procedure performed on himself. However, as his memories begin disappearing, he realizes that he does not actually want to forget Clementine.

Charlie Kaufman is no stranger to surreal and trippy stories. Paired with Michel Gondry's imaginative vision, Eternal Sunshine is the perfect marriage between romance and science fiction. The memory erasure plot is used as a representation of something people already do emotionally, like trying to escape painful experiences rather than accepting them. Even the structure mirrors the film's argument that by watching memories disappear, the audience comes to understand their value at the same time Joel does. Carrey turns in one of the best performances of his career, in a rare dramatic turn, and Winslet's Clementine is complex and interesting. It's not only one of the best sci-fi of the 21st century, but one of the best films ever.

'Her' (2013)

Image via Warner Bros. Pictures

Her follows Theodore Twombly (Joaquin Phoenix), a lonely writer struggling to move on from the breakdown of his marriage. His life changes when he gets an advanced operating system with an artificial intelligence named Samantha (Scarlett Johansson), an intelligent AI who develops a distinct personality and forms a romantic relationship with him.

Despite being released more than a decade ago, Her feels more relevant today. With AI now becoming ubiquitous in our lives, this film eerily predicts our current situation. The world is familiar and not too futuristic, a believable extension of contemporary society rather than an artificial science-fiction setting. Phoenix and Johansson also create a convincing relationship despite the fact that one character is never physically present in the traditional sense. Visually, Her is beautiful to watch, and it won Spike Jonze Best Original Screenplay at the Oscars.
